items.title: One-to-one counting
items.keyIdea: One-to-one correspondence means each object gets exactly one number name: touch or point once, say one word, then move on. Do not skip objects or say two numbers for the same object. The last number you say is how many there are.

items.title: How many in total?
items.keyIdea: The last number you say when counting tells you how many there are.

items.title: Addition as combining or putting together two
items.keyIdea: Addition means putting two groups together and finding how many there are altogether. The total keeps both amounts — nothing is thrown away.

items.title: Subtraction as taking away
items.keyIdea: Subtraction as taking away means start with a group, remove some, and count how many remain. The minus sign marks the take-away. Do not add the removed objects back, and do not count only what you removed as the answer for how many are left.

items.title: Reading +, −, and = symbols
items.keyIdea: The + sign means put together (add). The − sign means take away (subtract). The = sign means is the same as — both sides have the same value, not just “write the answer on the right”.

items.title: What the equals sign means
items.keyIdea: = means both sides are worth the same, like a balanced seesaw.

items.title: Multiplying as repeated adding
items.keyIdea: Multiplying is a quick way to add equal groups.

items.title: Dividing by sharing equally
items.keyIdea: Dividing means sharing fairly into equal groups.

items.title: Fraction words and notation
items.keyIdea: The denominator says how many equal parts the whole has; the numerator says how many of them you mean.

items.title: Fractions of amounts
items.keyIdea: To find a fraction of an amount, split it into equal groups, then take some of the groups.

items.title: Changes and separation words
items.keyIdea: Melt, freeze, evaporate and condense name changes of state; sieve, filter, evaporate and magnet name ways to separate mixtures.

items.title: Reversible changes
items.keyIdea: A reversible change can be undone: melting, freezing, dissolving and mixing make no new material.

items.title: Square and cube numbers
items.keyIdea: A square number is n × n (written n²); a cube number is n × n × n (written n³).

items.title: Slopes of parallel and perpendicular lines
items.keyIdea: Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to −1.

items.title: Pythagoras' theorem
items.keyIdea: In a right-angled triangle the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the longest side: a² + b² = c².

items.title: Probability as a fraction
items.keyIdea: When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of one outcome is 1 over the number of outcomes: a fair die gives 1/6 for each number.

items.title: Energy stores and transfers
items.keyIdea: Energy is never made or destroyed. It sits in stores (kinetic, thermal, chemical and more) and moves between them mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation.

items.title: Current and voltage
items.keyIdea: Current is how fast charge flows round a circuit, measured in amps with an ammeter in the loop. Voltage (potential difference) is the energy each charge gives up or gains, measured in volts with a voltmeter across a part.

items.title: Wave properties and types
items.keyIdea: A wave carries energy, not material. Speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f × λ). Transverse waves wiggle across the direction of travel; longitudinal waves wiggle along it.

items.title: Atomic number and mass number
items.keyIdea: The atomic number is the number of protons, and it decides the element. The mass number is protons plus neutrons. In a neutral atom the electrons equal the protons; an ion has gained or lost electrons.

items.title: Writing fraction facts
items.keyIdea: We can write fraction facts like 1/2 of 6 = 3, and different fractions can name the same amount.

items.title: Electron shells and configurations
items.keyIdea: Electrons fill shells from the inside out: 2 in the first shell, then 8, then 8 for the first 20 elements. The configuration, such as 2,8,1 for sodium, tells you the period (how many shells) and the group (how many outer electrons).

items.title: Covalent bonding
items.keyIdea: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Each atom shares enough pairs to fill its outer shell, so the number of bonds is usually 8 minus its outer electrons (hydrogen makes 1).

items.title: The unit circle
items.keyIdea: On the unit circle (radius 1, centre at the origin), the point reached by turning θ anticlockwise from the positive x-axis has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ). This defines sine and cosine for every angle, and the quadrant decides their signs.

items.title: Reading wave diagrams and graphs
items.keyIdea: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot of the whole wave at one instant, so the gap from crest to crest along it is the wavelength. A displacement–time graph follows one point as time passes, so the crest-to-crest gap is the period. On both, the amplitude is measured from the rest line up to a

items.title: Evaluating expressions with negative values
items.keyIdea: Put each value in brackets, then follow the order of operations. A power acts only on what it touches: for x = −3, x² = 9 but −x² = −9.

items.title: Factorising x² + bx + c
items.keyIdea: To factorise x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. They go in the brackets: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4), because 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7. Expand the brackets to check.

items.title: Expanding brackets with negatives
items.keyIdea: The number in front of a bracket multiplies every term inside it, and its sign goes with it. So −3(x − 4) = −3x + 12, because −3 × −4 = +12. In 5 − 2(x + 1) the multiplier is −2: 5 − 2x − 2 = 3 − 2x.

items.title: Equivalent expressions
items.keyIdea: Two expressions are equivalent when they give the same value for every x. One value where they differ proves they are not. A match at one value proves nothing, so to show they are equivalent, simplify both to the same form.

items.title: Why carbon forms so many compounds
items.keyIdea: Carbon has four outer electrons, so every carbon atom makes four covalent bonds. Carbon atoms also bond strongly to each other, in chains, branches and rings, so the same few atoms can be joined in millions of different ways.

items.title: Hydrocarbons
items.keyIdea: A hydrocarbon is a compound made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only. Size, double bonds and rings do not matter; one atom of any other element, such as oxygen or chlorine, means it is not a hydrocarbon.

items.title: Fractions on a number line
items.keyIdea: Fractions are numbers with their own place on the number line.

items.title: Molecular, structural and displayed formulae
items.keyIdea: One molecule can be written three ways. A displayed formula draws every atom and every bond. A structural formula lists the groups along the chain, such as CH₃CH₂CH₃. A molecular formula only counts the atoms, such as C₃H₈, so it loses the shape.

items.title: Alkanes
items.keyIdea: Alkanes are hydrocarbons with only single bonds. Every carbon makes four bonds and holds as many hydrogens as it can, so alkanes are saturated and all fit one general formula, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

items.title: Homologous series
items.keyIdea: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group and the same general formula. Neighbouring members differ by CH₂, they react in similar ways, and physical properties such as boiling point change gradually along the series.

items.title: Periodic table patterns from electrons
items.keyIdea: The periodic table is laid out by electrons. For main-group elements the group number equals the number of outer-shell electrons, and the period number equals the number of occupied shells. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways.

items.title: Alkenes
items.keyIdea: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with one carbon–carbon double bond, C=C. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ: ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆, butene C₄H₈. Because the double bond can open and take on more atoms, alkenes are unsaturated, and they turn orange bromine water colourless.

items.title: Simplifying algebraic fractions
items.keyIdea: Factorise the top and the bottom, then cancel any factor they share. (x² + 5x + 6)/(x + 2) = (x + 2)(x + 3)/(x + 2) = x + 3. Only whole factors cancel, never single terms, and any x that made the original bottom zero is still not allowed.

items.title: Instantaneous speed from curved graphs
items.keyIdea: On a distance–time graph the gradient is the speed. When the graph curves, the speed at one instant is the gradient of the tangent at that point: a straight line that just touches the curve there. Find it as rise ÷ run from a triangle on the tangent. Distance ÷ time from the start gives the average

items.title: Functional groups
items.keyIdea: A functional group is the atom or small group of atoms that gives an organic compound its typical reactions. The rest of the molecule is a carbon chain that hardly reacts. Four groups to know: C=C in alkenes, –OH in alcohols, –COOH in carboxylic acids and –COO– in esters. Compounds with the same gro

items.title: Noble gases and stable outer shells
items.keyIdea: The noble gases in Group 0 (helium, neon, argon and the rest) hardly react, because their outer shell of electrons is already full: 2 for helium, 8 for the others. Other atoms react in ways that give them the same full outer shell. Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them, and some atoms share th

items.title: Forming ions
items.keyIdea: An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons, so its protons and electrons no longer balance. Metals lose their outer electrons and become positive ions; non-metals gain electrons and become negative ions. The group number predicts the charge: groups 1, 2 and 3 give 1+, 2+ and 3+; groups 5, 6

items.title: Equivalent fractions
items.keyIdea: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount.

items.title: Chords, arcs, sectors, segments and tangents
items.keyIdea: A chord is a straight line joining two points on a circle; the diameter is the longest chord, through the centre. An arc is part of the curved edge: the minor arc is less than half, the major arc more. A sector is a region bounded by two radii and an arc; a segment is a region cut off by a chord. A

items.title: Rewriting expressions to reveal meaning
items.keyIdea: Equivalent forms of an expression give the same value but show different things. a + 0.05a shows the 5% added; 1.05a shows one multiplier that does the whole change. Pick the form that answers the question you were asked.

items.title: Arc length and sector area
items.keyIdea: A sector with angle θ is θ/360 of the circle. Its arc is that fraction of 2πr, and its area is that fraction of πr².

items.title: Radian measure
items.keyIdea: One radian is the angle at the centre when the arc is as long as the radius, so an angle in radians is arc ÷ radius: θ = s/r. About 6.28 radius-lengths fit round a circle, so a full turn is 2π rad and 180° = π rad. In radians the arc length is simply s = rθ.

items.title: Simplifying surds
items.keyIdea: √(a × b) = √a × √b, so a square factor can come out of the root: √72 = √36 × √2 = 6√2. Take out the biggest square factor. Like surds add like like terms, and 1/√2 = √2/2 after multiplying top and bottom by √2.

items.title: Exponential expressions: start value and growth factor
items.keyIdea: In a × bᵗ, a is the start value (the value at t = 0) and b is the factor you multiply by each step. A rise of r% gives b = 1 + r/100, a fall of r% gives b = 1 − r/100: +4% is × 1.04 and −15% is × 0.85.

items.title: Graphs of exponential functions
items.keyIdea: The graph of y = a × bˣ (a > 0) crosses the y-axis at (0, a). If b > 1 it rises ever more steeply (growth); if 0 < b < 1 it falls towards 0 (decay). It gets closer and closer to y = 0 but never touches it: y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote.

items.title: Naming organic compounds
items.keyIdea: An organic name is read in three parts. The stem counts the carbons in the longest chain: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-. The ending names the functional group: -ane, -ene, -ol or -oic acid. A number, counted from the end nearer the group, says which carbon it is on, as in propan-2-ol and but-1-ene.

items.title: Alcohols
items.keyIdea: Alcohols are the family with an –OH group on a carbon chain: methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol, CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. Their solutions in water are neutral. They fizz gently with sodium to give hydrogen, burn to carbon dioxide and water, and are oxidised to carboxylic acids. That makes them useful as fuel

items.title: Lengths in similar shapes
items.keyIdea: Similar shapes are the same shape at different sizes, so every length is multiplied by one scale factor k = new length ÷ matching old length. Match sides by the equal angles they sit opposite, pull overlapping triangles apart first, then multiply by k or solve a proportion.

items.title: Equations as a balance
items.keyIdea: Do the same thing to both sides and the equation stays balanced.

items.title: Why trigonometric ratios work
items.keyIdea: Every right triangle with the same acute angle θ has the same three angles, θ, 90° and 90° − θ, so they are all similar. Similar triangles keep their side ratios, so opposite ÷ hypotenuse, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and opposite ÷ adjacent depend only on θ. Those fixed numbers are sin θ, cos θ and tan θ.

items.title: Building a linear model from a context
items.keyIdea: When something changes by the same amount for every equal step, a straight line models it: output = start value + rate × input. Get the rate from two readings as change in output ÷ change in input, work back to input 0 for the start value, then say which inputs the model makes sense for.

items.title: Testing for alkenes with bromine water
items.keyIdea: Shake a few drops of orange bromine water with a liquid. If the orange turns colourless, the liquid has a C=C bond: bromine adds across it and is used up, so the compound is unsaturated. If it stays orange, there is no C=C. items.title: Exact trigonometric values
items.keyIdea: Two special triangles give exact values with no calculator. Halve an equilateral triangle of side 2 to get sides 1, √3 and 2 with angles 30°, 60° and 90°. items.title: Perfect squares and difference of squares
items.keyIdea: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², so the middle term is doubled. a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Root both parts first: 4x² − 25 = (2x + 5)(2x − 5).

items.title: Structural isomers
items.keyIdea: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but their atoms are bonded in a different order. Chain isomers have different carbon skeletons (butane and 2-methylpropane, both C₄H₁₀). Position isomers have the same group on a different carbon (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol). items.title: Acids, alkalis and hydrogen ions
items.keyIdea: In water, an acid releases hydrogen ions, H⁺, and an alkali releases hydroxide ions, OH⁻. Neutralisation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O; the other ions are spectators. Each step down the pH scale means ten times more H⁺, so pH 2 has 100 times the H⁺ of pH 4. A strong acid splits completely into ions; a weak acid

items.title: Halogens (Group 7)
items.keyIdea: The halogens are fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine. They exist as pairs of atoms (Cl₂, Br₂). Going down the group, melting and boiling points rise and colours darken: two gases, then a liquid, then a solid. Each atom has 7 outer electrons and reacts by gaining one. Reactivity falls down the gro

items.title: Carboxylic acids
items.keyIdea: Carboxylic acids contain the –COOH group: methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid have 1 to 4 carbons, counting the carbon in –COOH. items.title: Alkali metals (Group 1)
items.keyIdea: Lithium, sodium and potassium are soft, low-density metals with one outer electron. They tarnish quickly in air and react with water to give a metal hydroxide (an alkali) and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. They react by losing their outer electron to form 1+ ions. Reactivity increases down the g

items.title: Letters as numbers
items.keyIdea: In algebra a letter stands for a number, and 3a means 3 × a.

items.title: Understanding print
items.keyIdea: Print tells us something, and it says the same thing every time. In English we read from the top line down, and along each line from left to right. At the end of a line we jump back to the left. Gaps split the words, and each word is made of letters.

items.title: Naming Basic Emotions
items.keyIdea: Feelings have names. Four basic ones are happy, sad, angry and scared. Faces and bodies give clues: a happy mouth curves up; sad and angry mouths both turn down, but sad eyebrows go up in the middle while angry eyebrows pull down and together; a scared face has wide eyes and raised eyebrows. items.title: Writing digits 0-9
items.keyIdea: There are 10 digits, 0 to 9. Every digit starts at the top and follows the same path each time. Each digit faces one way (3, 7 and 9 are the ones most often turned round), sits on the line, and is as tall as a tall letter, so anyone can read it.

items.title: Asking for Help
items.keyIdea: When you are stuck, have a go first: try another way, then look for a clue. If you are still stuck, ask a friend or a grown-up, and say what you tried and what you need, such as a clue. If you are hurt, unsafe or someone is unkind, get a grown-up straight away. Asking after trying is what good learn

items.title: Spotting Patterns
items.keyIdea: A pattern is something that repeats or grows by a rule. Find the part that repeats, or the rule, and you can say what comes next. Test a rule on every step, not just the first one, and look for more examples before you are sure. Some patterns break, like run and ran, so check that your guess makes s

items.title: Writing Craft Vocabulary
items.keyIdea: Writers make choices on purpose, and craft words name those choices. Register is how formal or chatty the writing is, and the reader decides it. Purpose is why you write: to inform, persuade or entertain. Form is the kind of text, tone is the feeling, and cohesion is how the sentences link. Techniqu

items.title: Sitting and holding a pencil
items.keyIdea: Good writing starts before the pencil moves: feet flat, sit tall, and the other hand holds the paper. Pinch the pencil gently with thumb and pointer finger on the paint just above the wood, resting it on the middle finger. Most letters start at the top; e starts in the middle.

items.title: Persisting When It's Hard
items.keyIdea: Hard things get easier when you keep trying. A mistake is a clue that shows what to change, so try a different way instead of the same way again. Say "I can't do it yet", take a calm break if you feel cross, then have another go.

items.title: Question Words
items.keyIdea: Question words tell you what kind of answer is wanted: who asks about a person, what about a thing, where about a place, when about a time, why for a reason (often with because) and how about the way something happens. A question ends with a question mark.

items.title: Feelings Change and Differ
items.keyIdea: Everyone has feelings. Feelings change during a day, and big ones pass, often faster with a calm, kind way to cope. The same thing can make two people feel different things, because of what they like and what has happened to them before. Nobody's feeling is wrong, and we can be kind about a feeling

items.title: Order of operations
items.keyIdea: Brackets first, then × and ÷ (left to right), then + and − (left to right).

items.title: Listening and Responding
items.keyIdea: Good listening has three parts. Wait until the speaker has finished. Show you are listening with your eyes, a quiet mouth and still hands. Then give an answer that fits what was just said. In a group, put your hand up and wait to be asked, so everyone gets a turn.

items.title: Trends Across a Period and Down a Group
items.keyIdea: Across a period, protons are added but the inner shells stay the same, so the pull on the outer shell rises: atoms get smaller and their outer electrons get harder to remove. Down a group, each atom has an extra shell, so the outer electrons are further out and more shielded: atoms get bigger and th

items.title: Describing Rules and Testing Them
items.keyIdea: When you notice something happening again and again, say it as a rule that works every time: what you start with, what you do, and what happens. Then test the rule on new cases you have not seen, and hunt for a breaker. One breaker shows the rule is not always true, so fix it. Lots of examples help

items.title: Exploring Ideas Through Talk
items.keyIdea: Talk helps you think. Say "maybe" and "what if?" to get lots of ideas, not just one. Give a reason with "because" and a clue you can see. Test a what-if to find out. Try new words out loud, and add to a friend's idea with "yes, and".

items.title: Checking Your Own Work
items.keyIdea: When you finish, look back before you say done. Count again, touching each thing once. Read your writing back. Ask: does my answer fit the question? Check a sum another way. Fix any slips, then say what you checked.

items.title: Asking Questions
items.keyIdea: When you do not know, ask. Do not guess. A good question gets a clue or the real answer. When someone asks you, say just what they asked. If you did not get it, ask again kindly: can you say that again, please?

items.title: Inferring Characters' Feelings and Motives
items.keyIdea: Writers often show a feeling instead of naming it. You work it out from what a character does and says, and how they say it. That is an inference. A good inference fits every clue, and you can point to the exact words that prove it.

items.title: Skeletal formulae
items.keyIdea: A skeletal formula draws only the carbon chain as a zig-zag of lines. Every corner and every line end is a carbon. Hydrogens on carbon are not drawn: each carbon has four bonds, so it carries 4 minus the lines drawn to it. Other atoms, such as O in OH, are written in, and a double line is a C=C bond

items.title: Listening to Texts Read Aloud
items.keyIdea: When someone reads to you, listen for who is in it, where it happens and what goes wrong. Your answers come from the words you heard, not from your own life. You can tell the story back in order. If a word or part is not clear, ask the reader.

items.title: Words for Big Feelings
items.keyIdea: Big feelings have exact words: frustrated, disappointed, anxious and overwhelmed. Naming the feeling is the first step to handling it. Calm-down words name what helps: breathe slowly, use a strategy, cope, settle and have patience.

items.title: Writing equations from problems
items.keyIdea: Use a letter for the unknown number, then write what you know as an equation.

items.title: Teaching It Back
items.keyIdea: After you learn something, teach it back in your own words, to a person or even a toy. Say the idea, give an example you made up, and say why. Where you get stuck is a gap: now you know what to find out next.

items.title: Exploring with my five senses
items.keyIdea: You have five senses. Eyes see, ears hear, your nose smells, your mouth tastes and your hands feel. Use them to find out about things. Only taste food that a grown-up gives you.

items.title: Paying attention to one thing
items.keyIdea: Pick one thing and stay with it for a little while. Things will try to pull your eyes away. That is OK. Look back and keep going. A calm spot with just one thing out makes it easier.

items.title: Using and Evaluating Textual Evidence
items.keyIdea: Back up every point about a text with exact words from it. Strong evidence is about the thing you are claiming and fits only one reading. Keep quotations short, build them into your own sentence, then explain which words prove your point and how.

items.title: Animals and their babies
items.keyIdea: Animals have babies. A baby is a small one of the same kind of animal, and it grows into a grown-up like its mummy. Many babies have their own names: a lamb is a baby sheep, a calf is a baby cow, a kitten is a baby cat and a duckling is a baby duck.

items.title: All about me and my family
items.keyIdea: You can tell people about you: your name, how old you are, who lives with you, and what makes you special. Every family is different. A family can be big or small, with a mum, a dad, two dads, a gran or a pet, and each one is a real family.

items.title: How memory works
items.keyIdea: Working memory is a small desk that holds about four things at once. Long-term memory is a huge store. Forgetting is normal and fastest at first. Memories last longer when you recall them on spread-out days and link them to what you already know. Re-reading feels useful because the page looks famili

items.title: Emotion Vocabulary
items.keyIdea: There are many more feeling words than happy, sad, angry and scared. Some words are the same feeling at a different strength, like annoyed and furious. Some sound alike but mean different things: scared is about danger now, worried is about what might happen later. You can feel two things at once. T

items.title: Exam technique: command words and timing
items.keyIdea: The command word tells you what kind of answer earns marks: describe says what happens, explain gives reasons, compare covers both things, and evaluate weighs both sides and then judges. The marks in brackets tell you how much to write and how long to spend, about a minute a mark on many papers. Mar

items.title: Using help wisely, including AI tools
items.keyIdea: Good help leaves the thinking to you: hints, quizzes and explanations you then act on. AI tools can be fluent and wrong, so check their answers against something outside the AI, such as the question itself or a trusted source. In coursework, any AI use must be acknowledged, and copying or rewording

items.title: Using simple formulae
items.keyIdea: A formula is a rule for working something out: put the numbers in and follow the order of operations.

items.title: Supporting a friend who is struggling
items.keyIdea: A friend may be struggling when changes last for weeks and are not like them, such as dropping things they love, sleeping or eating differently, snapping, or saying there is no point. Listen more than you fix, ask open questions and encourage them to get help. Safety worries, like self-harm or wanti

items.title: Looking after your mental health
items.keyIdea: Low days are normal and usually lift within days. A low mood that lasts two weeks or more, or worry that is hard to control and gets in the way of life, is the time to get support. Sleep of 8 to 10 hours, regular activity and talking things through protect your mental health, while alcohol, avoidanc

items.title: Reading through critical lenses
items.keyIdea: A critical lens is a set of questions you bring to a text: Marxist critics ask about money, power and work; feminist critics about gender; postcolonial critics about empire; ecocritics about nature; psychoanalytic critics about hidden fears and wishes. One text can support many strong readings, but

items.title: E/Z isomerism
items.keyIdea: A C=C bond cannot rotate, because turning it would break the π bond. So when each carbon of the C=C carries two different groups, the groups are locked into two arrangements: E/Z isomers. items.title: Good stress and bad stress
items.keyIdea: Stress is your body's alarm. Adrenaline and cortisol make your heart race, your breathing speed up and your muscles tense, ready to act. Short stress that feels like a stretch you can handle, with an end in sight, can help you focus and perform: that is good stress. Stress that is too big, goes on f

items.title: Formal and informal English
items.keyIdea: We choose our words to suit the reader or listener, the purpose and the place. Informal English is chatty, for friends and family: Hi, grab, want to, See you, short forms like can't. Formal English is for people we do not know well or for serious jobs, like a letter to a headteacher or a talk to the

items.title: Electron sub-shells and orbitals
items.keyIdea: Each shell splits into sub-shells: s holds 2 electrons, p holds 6 and d holds 10. A sub-shell is made of orbitals, and one orbital holds at most 2 electrons with opposite spins. An s orbital is a sphere; a p sub-shell has three dumbbell-shaped orbitals at right angles. Electrons fill the lowest ener

items.title: Vocabulary: resilience and self
items.keyIdea: Resilience is bouncing back after a setback. A setback is something going wrong that slows you down for now. items.title: Plot Structure and Character Development
items.keyIdea: A plot is a chain of events with a shape. Tension rises to a turning point, the climax, then falls to a new normal. Along the way the main character is pushed to change, and that change is the character arc. The setting is not just a backdrop. It can cause the problem and force the choices.

items.title: Sigma and pi bonds
items.keyIdea: A σ (sigma) bond forms when two orbitals overlap end-on, so the shared electrons sit on the axis between the nuclei. items.title: Algebraic notation
items.keyIdea: Algebra drops the × sign: 3y means 3 × y, ab means a × b, a² means a × a, and a/b means a ÷ b.

items.title: Vocabulary: ethics and citizenship

items.title: Writing Process Vocabulary
items.keyIdea: Writers work in steps, and each step has a name. Plan means think of ideas and put them in order, the sequence. Draft means write it down, even if it is messy. items.keyIdea: In UV light, an alkane reacts with chlorine or bromine by substitution: a halogen atom replaces a hydrogen atom, and the hydrogen leaves as a hydrogen halide. items.title: The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
items.keyIdea: For every angle θ, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. It is Pythagoras on the unit circle: the point (cos θ, sin θ) is 1 from the origin. Rearranged as cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ, it turns one ratio into the other, with the quadrant fixing the sign, and it simplifies expressions.

items.title: Reading Shakespeare in context
items.keyIdea: Shakespeare's English is mostly our English, with a few old words to swap, such as thou for you and wherefore for why. items.title: Planning Narratives
items.keyIdea: Plan a story by borrowing methods from a mentor text, not its words. Show a character through action, speech and thought instead of naming the trait, choose setting details that build one mood, and move from a wide view to a close-up to build suspense.

items.title: Aldehydes, ketones and the carbonyl group
items.keyIdea: The carbonyl group C=O is polar: oxygen is more electronegative, so carbon is δ+ and oxygen δ−. In an aldehyde the C=O is at the end of the chain (–CHO, name ends -al); in a ketone it is inside the chain (–CO–, name ends -one). The δ+ carbon is where nucleophiles attack.

items.title: Sketching the gradient function

items.keyIdea: A haloalkane is an alkane with a halogen atom in place of a hydrogen, named with a prefix and a position number, as in 2-bromopropane. items.keyIdea: Replace each letter with its value, then calculate in the right order.

items.title: Playing alongside and together
items.keyIdea: Young children first play next to each other, each with their own toys, and that is normal. Step by step they start to play together: copying a friend, taking turns, passing a toy, asking "Can I play?" and sharing one game such as building a tower or rolling a ball.

items.title: Syllables
items.keyIdea: A syllable is one beat in a spoken word. Cat has one beat, rab-bit has two and but-ter-fly has three. items.title: Following two-step instructions
items.keyIdea: A two-step instruction asks for two things in order, such as "Get your shoes and bring them to the door." items.title: Vocabulary: social awareness
items.keyIdea: Eight words help you talk about how people are treated. A stereotype is a fixed idea about a whole group. Prejudice is judging one person before you know them, because of their group. Discrimination is treating someone unfairly because of their group: it is an action. Bias is a leaning for or agains

items.title: Floating and sinking
items.keyIdea: Put a thing in water and it either floats on top or sinks to the bottom. You cannot tell just from big or small: a big log floats and a tiny coin sinks. items.title: Knowing what you don't know
items.keyIdea: How sure you feel is a claim you can test. You are calibrated when your "70% sure" answers are right about 70% of the time. items.title: Money basics: budgeting and saving
items.keyIdea: A budget gives every pound a job before the month starts: needs first, then saving, then wants. Small regular costs add up to big yearly ones. Saving works best when it comes out first, on payday, and an emergency fund of about three months of essential costs stops one bad surprise turning into debt

items.title: Polar coordinates
items.keyIdea: A polar point (r, θ) is found by turning from the initial line by θ radians anticlockwise, then walking r units out from the pole. items.title: How a mass spectrometer works
items.keyIdea: A time-of-flight mass spectrometer has four stages. The sample is ionised, so the electric field can push it and the detector can register it. items.title: Habits and motivation
items.keyIdea: A habit is a loop: a cue triggers a routine, and a reward makes your brain want to repeat it. You build good habits by making them easy to start and linking them to a clear cue. Making bad habits awkward helps more than relying on willpower. Habits take weeks to feel automatic, often about two month

items.title: Using inverse operations
items.keyIdea: + undoes −, and × undoes ÷, so you can work backwards and check your answers.

items.title: Living and not living
items.keyIdea: Living things eat or drink, grow, and move or change by themselves. People, animals and plants are alive. Rocks, toys and cars are not. Moving is not enough: a toy robot moves, but it cannot eat or grow. Staying still does not mean dead: a tree and a sleeping cat are alive.

items.title: Rules that keep us safe
items.keyIdea: Some rules are there to stop us getting hurt. Hold a grown-up's hand by the road, because cars are big and fast. Walk, do not run, inside, so we do not trip and bump. items.title: Narrative perspective and unreliable narrators
items.keyIdea: Who tells a story decides what the reader can know. First person gives one mind from inside, third limited follows one mind from outside, and omniscient opens every mind. Narrators can also be wrong or lie, so test what they say against what happens.

items.title: Odd and even functions
items.keyIdea: A function is even when f(−x) = f(x) for every x: its graph is its own mirror image in the y-axis. It is odd when f(−x) = −f(x) for every x: a half turn about the origin leaves its graph unchanged. Most functions are neither. To test one, work out f(−x) and compare it with f(x) and with −f(x).

items.title: Quoting Accurately from Texts
items.keyIdea: A quotation is the writer's exact words, copied word for word and put inside quotation marks. Quote only the words that prove your point, whether the text says it outright or gives a clue you infer from. items.title: Shapes of molecules
items.keyIdea: Pairs of electrons round a central atom repel, so they spread out in 3D as far apart as they can. Count the regions: each bond counts once, even a double bond, and each lone pair counts too. Two regions give a linear shape (180°), three give trigonal planar (120°) and four give tetrahedral (109.5°).

items.title: Discussing and Questioning New Words
items.keyIdea: When you meet a word you do not know, stop and ask: what does it mean? Look for clues in the picture and in the words around it. items.title: Building on Others in Discussions
items.keyIdea: A good discussion grows. Instead of repeating what someone said, you build on it: keep their idea and add something new, such as a reason, an example or a fact. items.title: Communication Vocabulary
items.keyIdea: There are three ways to speak up. Passive means you go quiet or give in, so no one hears what you need. items.title: Expanding single brackets
items.keyIdea: Multiply everything inside the bracket by the term outside: 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15.

items.title: Reading for Meaning
items.keyIdea: Reading is not just saying the words. Reading means you get what the words mean. As you read, ask: does it make sense? Can I see a picture of it in my head? If it sounds silly, stop and read it again. When you finish, try to tell it back.

items.title: Partial fractions
items.keyIdea: Partial fractions splits one fraction into a sum of simpler ones, which is adding fractions in reverse. Each linear factor (x − a) in the denominator gets its own A/(x − a). items.title: Sorting & Categorising Words
items.keyIdea: Words can be put into groups. Things of the same kind go together, like animals or food. To sort, pick a rule and check every card against it. Change the rule and the groups change. Some words come in pairs of opposites, like big and small: an opposite is at the other end, not nearly the same.

items.title: Domain Vocabulary Across Subject Areas
items.keyIdea: Each subject has its own exact words, like numerator in maths, photosynthesis in science and parliament in history. items.title: Velocity and acceleration by differentiation
items.keyIdea: For motion in a straight line, velocity is the rate of change of displacement and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². items.title: Saying number names in order
items.keyIdea: Counting words always come in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, then six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Say every number once, with no skips and no repeats. Songs, rhymes and stairs help the order stick. You can count back too: five, four, three, two, one.

items.title: Triggers and Causes of Feelings
items.keyIdea: Feelings have causes. Something happens (a trigger) and then we feel a certain way: I felt sad because my balloon popped. items.title: How Emotions Feel in Your Body
items.keyIdea: Feelings show up in the body as clues. items.keyIdea: Capital letters are tall: every capital touches the top line and sits on the base line, and none hang below it. items.title: Writing expressions from words
items.keyIdea: Translate phrase by phrase, and watch the order for subtraction and division.

items.title: Parametric equations of curves
items.keyIdea: A parametric curve gives x and y separately in terms of a parameter t: x = f(t), y = g(t). Each value of t gives one point, so you can plot the curve from a table of t values. items.keyIdea: English comes in many varieties. A dialect is the English of a place or group, with its own words and grammar: wee and bairn in Scotland, nowt in Yorkshire, y'all in the southern USA. items.keyIdea: Feelings change the choices we make. When a feeling is very strong, like fury or panic, we notice fewer options and grab the fastest one, such as a mean reply. items.keyIdea: A chiral carbon is bonded to four different groups. A molecule with one chiral carbon has two forms that are mirror images but cannot be superimposed, however you turn them. items.title: Big and small, long and short
items.keyIdea: Big things take up lots of room and small things take up a little. Tall things go up high, and long things go a long way along. To compare fairly, start both things at the same line, then look at the other end. Put three things in order by starting with the smallest.

items.title: Learning by watching and copying
items.keyIdea: You can learn a new thing by watching someone do it and then copying them. Keep your eyes on the one who shows you, watch all the way to the end, then do the same steps in the same order. If you miss a bit, ask to see it again, slowly.

items.title: Main Topic of Informational Texts
items.keyIdea: A fact book or page has a main topic: the one thing every sentence tells about. Facts that tell about the topic are key details; things someone likes are not. You can say the main topic in one sentence, retell a few key facts, and use words like so to show how two facts are linked.

items.title: Author's word choices
items.keyIdea: Authors pick each word on purpose. items.keyIdea: Pronouns such as he, she, it and they stand in for a noun so you do not repeat it. items.title: Simple Calming Strategies
items.keyIdea: A big feeling is like a storm inside your body. You can make it smaller with a calm tool: breathe in, then let the air out slowly; count to ten slowly; or go to a safe, quiet place where a grown-up knows you are. items.title: Naming parts of my body
items.keyIdea: Your body has parts with names. Your head is at the top, your tummy is in the middle, and your toes are at the bottom on your feet. Arms bend at the elbow and legs bend at the knee. Each part helps you do things: legs help you walk, hands help you clap, your mouth helps you eat and arms give a hug.

items.title: Testing yourself: retrieval practice
items.keyIdea: Retrieval practice means pulling what you learned out of your memory, with the notes shut, and then checking. Each time you recall a fact, it gets easier to recall next time. items.title: Choosing the Right Coping Strategy
items.keyIdea: A coping strategy is a tool for a big feeling. Different feelings need different tools: hot, fast anger needs cooling down, and heavy sadness needs comfort and company. items.keyIdea: A book has a front cover with the title and a picture, a spine down the side, and a back cover with the blurb, which tells you what the book is about. items.title: Small changes and linear approximation

items.title: Fitting shapes into holes
items.keyIdea: Each shape fits the hole that matches it: round in round, square in square, triangle in triangle. If a shape is the right one but will not go in, turn it until its straight sides and corners line up with the hole. A circle has no corners, so it fits any way round, and it is the shape that rolls.

items.title: Basic Nouns & Verbs
items.keyIdea: A noun is a naming word: it names a person, a place or a thing, like girl, park or cup. A verb is a doing word: it tells what someone or something does, like run, eat or sleep. A simple sentence often has a noun that says who, then a verb that says what they do: The dog barks.

items.title: Things I like and things I can do
items.keyIdea: Your likes belong to you. You can say what you like and what you do not like, and that is OK. Friends like some things the same and some things different. You can do lots of jobs by yourself, and you ask a grown-up when a job is hot, fast or not safe.

items.title: Seeing 1, 2 or 3 at a glance
items.keyIdea: You can see one, two or three things fast, without counting. A quick look is enough. Moving things apart does not change how many. Big or tiny, each thing is one.

items.title: Word problems with linear equations
items.keyIdea: Name the unknown, write an equation, solve it, then check the answer makes sense.

items.title: Looking closely and noticing changes
items.keyIdea: Scientists look closely and notice what changes. Say what it was like before and what it is like now. Some changes are fast, like ice melting. Some are slow, like a banana going brown.

items.title: Remembering what comes next
items.keyIdea: A routine is the same steps in the same order, every day. Think: what did I just do, and what comes next? Some steps must come first, like socks before shoes. The more you do a routine, the less you need reminders.

items.title: Why the author wrote it
items.keyIdea: Every text has an author's purpose: to persuade you, to inform you, or to entertain you. items.title: Shades of Meaning

items.title: Long multiplication

items.title: Fact vs opinion
items.keyIdea: A fact is a statement that can be checked: measured, counted, observed or looked up in a reliable source. An opinion is what someone thinks, feels or believes, so it cannot be proved. items.title: Vocabulary: making decisions and keeping safe
items.keyIdea: A choice is when you pick what to do. A consequence is what happens because of that choice, and it can be good or bad. A rule tells everyone what to do so we stay safe and are fair. items.title: Being gentle with people, animals and plants

items.title: Matching pairs

items.title: Breaking Tasks into Steps
items.keyIdea: A big job feels hard to start because you see all of it at once. Break it into small, clear steps, put them in a sensible order, and start the first one now. If a step still feels too big, break it again. After each step, notice your progress: one done, on to the next.

items.keyIdea: Divide, then decide what the remainder means: leftover, fraction, decimal, or round up or down.

items.title: Melting and freezing
items.keyIdea: Warming makes ice melt into water. Cooling makes water freeze into ice. Ice is a solid: it keeps its shape. Water is a liquid: it flows and takes the shape of its cup. The warmer the place, the faster ice melts, and melted ice can freeze again, so this change goes both ways.

items.title: Day, night and the seasons
items.keyIdea: In the day the sky is light and we see the sun. At night it is dark and we see the moon and stars. The sun comes up in the morning, is high at midday and goes down in the evening. items.keyIdea: When words do not make sense, your brain gives you a "huh?" feeling. Good learners notice that feeling and stop, instead of reading or listening past it. Then they fix it: read it again, look at the picture, slow down, or ask "What does that mean?"

items.keyIdea: If the way you are trying is not working, doing it again the same way usually gives the same result. items.keyIdea: Helpful feedback is about the work, not the person, and it is specific: it names one thing that worked (a star) and one thing to try next (a step). items.keyIdea: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving. It increases in proportion to mass: twice the mass at the same speed means twice the kinetic energy. items.keyIdea: A prediction is a guess about what will happen next in a story. A good prediction uses clues: the title, the pictures, and what has happened so far. items.keyIdea: You keep changing as you grow. Things that were hard at six are easy now, so the things that are hard now are not fixed either. items.keyIdea: Memory fades fast after you study, then more slowly: the forgetting curve. items.title: The periodic table
items.keyIdea: Elements are arranged by atomic number in rows (periods) and columns (groups). Elements in a group have similar properties.

items.title: Reading Between the Lines

items.keyIdea: Reflecting on a friendship means looking at your own part, not only at what others do. items.keyIdea: The model of the atom changed each time new evidence did not fit. Dalton's solid spheres (1803) gave way to Thomson's plum pudding (1897) when the electron was found. items.keyIdea: Some sounds you already know have a new spelling in certain words. The or sound is spelled a before l or ll (all, ball, walk, talk). items.title: Grammar Terms: Voice and Punctuation
items.keyIdea: Year 6 writers use exact terms. The subject is who or what a sentence is about; the object receives the action of the verb. items.title: Statistical questions and variability
items.keyIdea: A statistical question is one that expects variability in the answers: How many pets do pupils in my class have? is statistical, but How old am I? has one answer and is not. items.title: Counting in 2s
items.keyIdea: Counting in 2s means jumping 2 each time: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Counting in 5s goes 5, 10, 15, 20, and counting in 10s goes 10, 20, 30. Keep the same jump every time. The last number you say tells how many things there are, not how many groups.

items.title: Making Loud and Quiet Sounds
items.keyIdea: You make a sound when you hit, shake or blow something. Hit, shake or blow hard and the sound is loud. Do it gently and the sound is quiet. High and low are different from loud and quiet: a tiny bell rings high, a big bell rings low.

items.title: Drawing to Help Me Think
items.keyIdea: Putting words and a picture together helps you understand and remember. A thinking picture can be a quick sketch, a diagram with labels, or a timeline that shows what happens in order. It should be quick and simple, and show the idea, not decoration.

items.title: Numbers up to 10 into pairs
items.keyIdea: A number can be split into two parts in more than one way. 6 is 1 and 5, 2 and 4, or 3 and 3. These pairs are number bonds. The two parts together make the whole. items.title: Counting atoms in formulae
items.keyIdea: A small number after a symbol counts that atom. A big number in front counts whole molecules. Brackets multiply everything inside.

items.title: Hot, warm and cold
items.keyIdea: Things can feel hot, warm or cold. Ice and snow are cold. A bath and baby milk should be warm. Fire, an oven and a full teapot are hot, and hot things can burn, even when they do not look hot. Hot things left out cool down. Warmth makes ice melt, and cold keeps it frozen.

items.title: Computers in Everyday Life
items.keyIdea: A computer is a machine that follows instructions. Something goes in, the computer follows its steps, and something comes out. Computers are not just laptops. items.title: Perimeters of polygons
items.keyIdea: The perimeter is the total distance all the way round the edge of a flat shape. Add the lengths of every side and keep the unit, such as cm or m. items.title: Mould and mushrooms (fungi)
items.keyIdea: Mushrooms, toadstools and mould are living things called fungi. One of them is a fungus. Fungi are not plants: they have no green leaves and do not make food from sunlight. items.title: Deliberate practice
items.keyIdea: Deliberate practice is practice designed to improve one specific weakness. items.title: A Ten Is Ten Ones
items.keyIdea: Ten ones can be bundled into one group called a ten. A ten rod is 10 cubes stuck together, so 1 ten and 10 ones are the same amount. items.title: Conductors and insulators
items.keyIdea: An electrical conductor is a material that lets electricity flow through it, so it completes a circuit and the bulb lights. items.title: Figurative Language and Literary Devices
items.keyIdea: Writers choose words for their connotations, the feelings they carry, as well as their meanings: slim and scrawny both mean thin but feel different. items.title: 3-D shapes
items.keyIdea: A 3-D shape is a solid you can hold, not a flat drawing. A cube has 6 flat faces that are all the same square; a cuboid is a stretched cube with some long rectangle faces. items.title: Playing with what I know
items.keyIdea: In pretend play a young child uses what they already know from real life. items.title: Conservation of mass
items.keyIdea: In any change, the total mass stays the same, as long as nothing gets in or out.

items.title: Choosing Form and Tone for Your Audience
items.keyIdea: Before writing, ask who the audience is and what the purpose is: to inform, persuade, entertain or instruct. items.title: Changing Shapes of Solids
items.keyIdea: You can change the shape of some solid objects by squashing, stretching, bending or twisting them. Each one is a push or a pull. items.keyIdea: A factor of a number goes into it exactly, with nothing left over. items.keyIdea: Young children learn by having their own ideas and trying them out, not only by copying. items.keyIdea: A line of symmetry is a fold line: fold the shape on it and one half lands exactly on the other. items.keyIdea: Air is all around us, even though we cannot see it. items.keyIdea: A healthy relationship rests on respect, trust, honesty and the freedom to say no. Relationships sit on a spectrum from healthy to unhealthy to abusive. items.keyIdea: Dry sand pours and runs, like water does, so a dry sand castle falls down into a heap. items.keyIdea: An analogue clock has two hands. The short hand is the hour hand: it points to the hour. items.keyIdea: In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged into new substances. No atoms are created or destroyed.

items.keyIdea: When you mix things, something changes. Flour and water stirred together turn into soft dough. items.title: Ordering Events in Time
items.keyIdea: Things happen in an order. Time words tell us that order. First, next and last say which thing comes when. Before means earlier and after means later. A day goes morning, then afternoon, then evening. Yesterday was the day before today, and tomorrow is the day after today.

items.keyIdea: To compare two books, look at both together. Find what is the same and what is different: theme, characters, setting and how the story is told. items.keyIdea: A word equation names the reactants, then an arrow meaning 'react to make', then the products.

items.keyIdea: Every sound is made by something vibrating. Pitch is how high or low a sound is, and it depends on how fast the object vibrates: faster vibrations make a higher pitch. items.keyIdea: Germs are tiny living things, far too small to see, and some of them can make us ill. They spread from our hands to everything we touch, and from sneezes and coughs. items.title: Herbivores, Carnivores & Omnivores
items.keyIdea: We can sort animals by what they eat. A herbivore eats only plants, like a cow or a rabbit. A carnivore eats only meat, like a lion or a cat. items.keyIdea: Camouflage is when an animal's colour or pattern helps it blend in with its habitat, so it is hard to see. items.keyIdea: A force diagram shows each force on an object as a labelled arrow. The arrow points the way the force acts, and its length shows the size of the force, drawn to scale (for example 1 square = 10 newtons). items.keyIdea: Energy is what makes things happen, and it has names. It can be stored: chemical energy in food and batteries, elastic energy in a stretched band, gravitational energy in something lifted up. items.keyIdea: Many things at home need electricity to work. Some plug into a wall socket and use mains electricity. Others, like a torch or a remote, use batteries. items.title: Nets of 3-D Shapes
items.keyIdea: A net is a flat 2-D pattern that folds into a 3-D shape. The faces of the solid are drawn joined edge to edge so that when you fold along the edges, every face meets without overlapping. A cube net has 6 equal squares; only some arrangements of 6 squares fold into a cube. A cuboid net has 6 rectangl

items.title: Drawing Life Cycle Diagrams
items.keyIdea: A life cycle diagram shows the stages of a living thing in order, drawn in a circle with arrows, because the young grow up and the cycle begins again. A butterfly goes egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult. A frog goes spawn → tadpole → froglet → adult frog. A flowering plant goes see

items.title: The definite integral
items.keyIdea: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx is what the sum of strip areas settles on as the strips get thinner: the signed area.

items.title: The Heart and Blood
items.keyIdea: Your heart is a muscle in your chest that pumps blood all the time. Each squeeze pushes blood out through tubes called blood vessels to every part of your body, from your head to your toes, and the blood comes back to the heart in other blood vessels. You can feel each squeeze as a heartbeat: put a

items.title: Telling Time to Five Minutes
items.keyIdea: The long hand is the minute hand. From one number to the next is 5 minutes, so count the long hand in 5s from the 12: the 1 is 5 minutes past, the 3 is 15 (quarter past), the 6 is 30 (half past) and the 9 is 45 (quarter to the next hour). On the right of the clock we say minutes past the hour; on th

items.title: Equations with Two Unknowns
items.keyIdea: An equation with two unknowns, such as a + b = 10, usually has many solutions: each solution is a pair of numbers (a, b) that makes the equation true. To find them all, work systematically: try a = 0, 1, 2 and so on, and work out b each time. Order matters, so (3, 7) and (7, 3) are different pairs.

items.title: How fossils form
items.keyIdea: A fossil is the shape of something that once lived, trapped inside rock. First the plant or animal dies and gets buried in mud or sand. More layers pile on. Over millions of years that soft mud hardens into rock, and the shape stays inside. Digging later can reveal a shell, bone, leaf imprint or foo

items.title: The teen numbers
items.keyIdea: Teen numbers from 11 to 19 are one full ten and some leftover ones. Fourteen is a ten-frame filled plus four more: 10 + 4. Seventeen is 10 + 7. Seeing teens this way is early place value: the 1 in 14 stands for one ten, and the 4 stands for four ones.

items.title: Number Bonds to 10
items.keyIdea: Number bonds to 10 are pairs of numbers that add to exactly 10: 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6, 5+5 and the same pairs swapped. If 7 counters fill a ten-frame, 3 spaces stay empty, so 7 and 3 are partners. Knowing these pairs lets you make 10 quickly without counting every time.

items.title: Turns and Directions
items.keyIdea: A turn is measured by how much of a whole circle you go round. items.title: What is a minibeast?
items.keyIdea: A minibeast is a small animal with no backbone, such as a beetle, spider, woodlouse, snail or worm. Animals with no backbone are called invertebrates. You find minibeasts on a bug hunt by looking gently under logs, stones and leaves and using a hand lens to see them up close. Insects have 6 legs and

items.title: Persuasive Writing: Building an Argument
items.keyIdea: A written argument states a claim (a view someone could disagree with), supports it with reasons and relevant evidence, acknowledges a counterclaim fairly and rebuts it, links ideas with words such as furthermore, however and therefore, keeps a formal style, and ends with a concluding statement that

items.title: Counting in 6s
items.keyIdea: Counting in 6s adds 6 each time: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60, 66, 72. These are the multiples of 6, the answers in the 6 times table. Every multiple of 6 is even, and the ones digits repeat 6, 2, 8, 4, 0. A 6 is two 3s, so the 6s are every second number in the 3s count and 6 × n is double

items.title: Where water is found on Earth
items.keyIdea: Water is found in oceans and seas, in rivers, lakes and ponds, frozen in glaciers, ice sheets and snow, under the ground and in clouds. Almost all of it, about 97 of every 100 cups, is salty ocean water. Only about 3 cups are fresh, and most of that fresh water is frozen ice. Fresh water under the g

items.title: Mixing up practice: interleaving
items.keyIdea: Interleaving means mixing different types of problem in one practice session, so each question makes you decide which method to use. Blocked practice (one type at a time) feels smoother and scores higher during practice, but interleaved practice usually leaves far more a week later. Mix types that l

items.title: Fluent adding and subtracting within 5
items.keyIdea: Fluent within 5 means you know every add and take-away with numbers 0 to 5 straight away — 2 + 3 = 5, 5 − 2 = 3, 4 + 0 = 4 — without counting each finger every time. Subitising (seeing a small group at a glance) and a five-frame help. Facts past 5, like 3 + 3 = 6, are outside this set.

items.title: Reading and writing numbers to 20
items.keyIdea: Reading a numeral means knowing which written mark stands for a count from 0 to 20. Writing means making those digits in the right order: tens on the left, ones on the right. Teen numbers are one ten and some ones — 14 is 1 ten and 4 ones. Swapping digits changes the number: 12 is twelve, 21 is twen

items.title: What Living Things Need
items.keyIdea: Living things need water, food, air and suitable conditions to stay alive. Animals get food by eating; plants make food using light. A need is required for survival; a want (toys, TV) is optional. A fish needs a watery place; a cactus needs a dry, sunny place — the wrong place is not suitable.

items.title: Whales & Dolphins Are Mammals
items.keyIdea: Whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish. They breathe air at the surface, are warm-blooded, and feed babies milk. Living in the ocean does not make an animal a fish — fish usually use gills and do not feed milk.

items.title: How Breathing Works
items.keyIdea: Air goes in through the nose or mouth, down the windpipe, into the lungs. Lungs take oxygen the body needs. We breathe out carbon dioxide waste. The chest rises on breathe-in and falls on breathe-out.

items.title: Relative formula mass
items.keyIdea: Relative formula mass Mr is the sum of the relative atomic masses Ar of every atom in a formula. Count atoms carefully when brackets multiply a group (Ca(OH)₂ → Ca + 2O + 2H). Percentage by mass of an element = (total Ar of that element ÷ Mr) × 100.

items.title: Reading ×, ÷, and = Symbols
items.keyIdea: The multiply sign × means equal groups (2 × 3 is two groups of three). The divide sign ÷ means share equally (6 ÷ 2 is 6 shared into 2 groups). The equals sign = means both sides have the same value — not only "write the answer on the right".

items.title: Dinosaurs Were Real
items.keyIdea: Dinosaurs were real animals that lived on Earth long ago — millions of years before people. Fossils (bones, teeth, footprints and eggs in rock) are the evidence. Toy dinosaurs and story dragons are not fossils.

items.title: Evaluating definite integrals
items.keyIdea: Integrate, write [F(x)] with the limits, then work out F(top) − F(bottom); the result is signed area.

items.title: What Is a Volcano
items.keyIdea: A volcano is a mountain or hill with a hole (vent) where hot melted rock from under the ground can come out. Melted rock under the ground is magma. When it flows out it is called lava. An eruption is when magma, ash or gas bursts out.

items.title: Representing Numbers with Objects
items.keyIdea: A numeral stands for a count (cardinality). Represent it by placing exactly that many objects. Matching collections share the same count, even if the objects look different. The digit shape is a symbol — do not count its loops.

items.title: Measuring Length and Height
items.keyIdea: Length is how long something is along a line. Height is how tall it stands. To compare fairly, line up the starting ends. Measure with the same non-standard unit end to end — no gaps or overlaps.

items.title: What Is the Ocean?
items.keyIdea: The ocean is a huge body of salt water that covers most of Earth. It has a shore, shallow water and deep water. It is a habitat for sea animals. Puddles, baths and swimming pools are not oceans.

items.title: Common Plants & Trees
items.keyIdea: Name common wild and garden plants (daisy, grass, rose, dandelion, oak, holly). Deciduous trees lose their leaves in autumn; evergreen trees keep green leaves all year. Match a plant to its name from a picture or clue.

items.title: Capacity and volume
items.keyIdea: Capacity is how much a container can hold when full. Measure it by counting equal cups that fill it, then record a number with a unit (cups, and litres for larger jugs). Taller does not always mean more; how full right now is not capacity.

items.title: Wild, Farm & Pet Animals
items.keyIdea: Animals fit three care groups: wild animals find their own food and shelter in nature and should be watched from a safe distance; farm animals are kept by people for food, wool or eggs; pets are kept for companionship and need people to feed and care for them every day.

items.title: Measuring mass and weight
items.keyIdea: Mass is how heavy something is. Measure it by balancing equal cubes until both sides level, then record a number with a unit (for example 4 cubes). Simple scales can also show grams. Bigger is not always heavier — measure, do not guess from size alone.

items.title: Displacement and velocity by integration
items.keyIdea: Displacement is the integral of velocity, and velocity is the integral of acceleration; starting values fix the constants.

items.title: Nocturnal Animals
items.keyIdea: Nocturnal animals are active at night and usually asleep in the day. Many have big eyes, big ears or sensitive whiskers to find food in the dark. Owls, bats and hedgehogs are nocturnal; not every animal sleeps when the sun goes down.

items.title: Transparent, Translucent & Opaque
items.keyIdea: Materials treat light in three ways. Transparent materials let you see clearly through them. Translucent materials let some light through but the view is blurry. Opaque materials block light so you cannot see through them.

items.title: Counting objects to 20
items.keyIdea: Count each object once, say the number names in order, and stop at the target. The last number you say is how many objects there are — even when you count past ten into the teens.

items.title: Types of Weather
items.keyIdea: Weather types name what the sky and air are doing today: sunny, rainy, cloudy, windy or snowy. Watch for clues like bright sun, falling drops, thick cloud, pushing air or cold white flakes.

items.title: Naming the Planets
items.keyIdea: Eight planets orbit our Sun in a fixed order from closest to farthest: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. A star makes its own light; a planet orbits a star; a moon orbits a planet.

items.title: Animals Everywhere
items.keyIdea: Animals live all over the world — on land, in water and in the air — and every continent, even icy Antarctica, is home to animals suited to the conditions where they live.

items.title: Inverse: addition undoes subtraction
items.keyIdea: Addition and subtraction undo each other. You can check a sum by subtracting, and solve missing-number problems with the inverse.

items.title: What Is a Rainforest?
items.keyIdea: A rainforest is a thick, tall forest in hot, wet places near the Equator where it rains almost every day, so plants grow tall and dense.

items.title: A Hundred Is Ten Tens
items.keyIdea: One hundred is ten tens. In place value, the hundreds digit counts groups of 100 — ten rods of ten make one hundred flat.

items.title: Observation vs Interpretation
items.keyIdea: An observation is what you see, hear, or measure. An interpretation is a guess about why or what it means. Keep them separate so claims rest on evidence.

items.title: Types of chemical reaction
items.keyIdea: Combustion is burning in oxygen; oxidation is gaining oxygen; thermal decomposition breaks a substance down with heat; displacement swaps in a more reactive metal.

items.title: Estimating by rounding
items.keyIdea: Round each number to a nearby ten, then calculate. The result is an estimate — close and quick, not always exact.

items.title: Two written numerals between 1 and 10
items.keyIdea: Compare two written numerals from 1 to 10 by their value: which is greater, which is less. How tall the digit looks does not change the number.

items.title: Commutative Multiplication
items.keyIdea: Multiplication is commutative: a×b = b×a. Flipping an array changes its shape, not how many dots you have.

items.title: What Is an Earthquake
items.keyIdea: An earthquake is the ground shaking when pieces of Earth's crust (plates) bump, scrape, or slide. Stay safe with Drop, Cover, Hold.

items.title: The multiples of 100
items.keyIdea: Multiples of 100 (100–900) are whole hundreds: a hundreds digit with 0 tens and 0 ones. 300 means 3 hundreds, not 3 tens.

items.title: The Five Oceans
items.keyIdea: Earth has five named oceans — Pacific (largest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic (smallest and coldest) — that form one connected global ocean.

items.title: Rote counting to 100
items.keyIdea: Rote counting is saying number names in order from 0 to 100 — forwards, backwards, or starting from any number — without skipping or repeating.

items.title: How Plant Parts Work
items.keyIdea: Each plant part has a job: roots take in water and minerals, the stem carries them up, leaves make food with light, and flowers help make seeds.

items.title: Sorting into categories
items.keyIdea: Put objects into the given groups, count how many are in each group, then order the groups from most to least.

items.title: Forces Vocabulary
items.keyIdea: Forces have clear names: push and pull; stretch, squash and twist for shape; touch forces versus gravity and magnets; friction and air resistance that slow things down.

items.title: Physical vs chemical changes
items.keyIdea: A physical change makes no new substance and is usually reversible; a chemical change makes new substances. Mass is conserved in both.

items.title: Number bonds
items.keyIdea: Number bonds within 20 are pairs of numbers that add to a total up to 20, plus the related subtraction fact. If 8 + 7 = 15, then 15 − 7 = 8. Quick recall of these bonds means you do not recount from one every time.

items.title: Representing Addition and Subtraction
items.keyIdea: Addition and subtraction can be represented with objects, drawings, and mental images such as fingers — not only with written number sentences. Showing 3 + 2 with cubes, a sketch, or raised fingers is the same sum.

items.title: Fluent adding and subtracting within 10
items.keyIdea: Fluent within 10 means you know every addition and subtraction fact with numbers 0–10 straight away — ten-frame pictures, make-10 bridges, and related take-aways — without recounting every counter.

items.title: Water Transport in Plants
items.keyIdea: Water enters at the roots, travels up thin tubes in the stem, and reaches the leaves. A blocked stem stops the path so leaves above dry out — the celery-dye model makes the pathway visible.

items.title: Telling time to the minute (age 7+)
items.keyIdea: Every small mark on the clock is one minute. Read times like 3:17 and 5:42 — minutes past before half past, and minutes to the next hour after half past — and match the digital form.

items.title: Addition and subtraction within 20
items.keyIdea: Within 20 you use strategies — make ten then add the rest, decompose a take-away so you hit ten first, count on from the larger number, and use related facts — not only snap recall of facts within 10.

items.title: Animal Nutrition
items.keyIdea: Animals, including humans, need the right types and amounts of nutrition from food they eat — they cannot make their own food the way green plants can.

items.title: Choosing measurement units
items.keyIdea: Pick the unit that fits what you measure: cm or m for length, g or kg for mass, °C for temperature, ml or litres for capacity — not one unit for everything.

items.title: The three digits of a three-digit number
items.keyIdea: In a three-digit number the digits stand for hundreds, tens and ones — so 347 means 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 7 ones, not 3+4+7 and not a swap of places.

items.title: The two digits of a two-digit number
items.keyIdea: In a two-digit number the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones — so 47 means 4 tens + 7 ones (forty-seven), not 4+7 and not 7 tens.

items.title: Irreversible changes
items.keyIdea: Some changes make new materials that cannot easily be turned back, like burning, rusting and acid reactions.

items.title: Pollination & Seed Dispersal
items.keyIdea: Flowers make pollen on anthers; pollination moves pollen to a stigma so a seed can form; seeds then disperse (wind, animals, water, bursting) so new plants have space — not only so flowers look pretty.

items.title: Mean absolute deviation
items.keyIdea: The mean absolute deviation (MAD) is the average of how far each value sits from the mean: for each value find |value − mean|, then average those absolute deviations. Same mean can hide very different MAD; MAD measures typical distance from the centre, not the range and not the mean itself.

items.title: Organising homework and deadlines
items.keyIdea: Organising homework means writing every task down with its due date, estimating how long each needs, breaking big tasks into steps, and placing them into a planner so nothing relies on memory alone. Due-soon and high-stakes work gets protected time first; 'I'll remember' and 'easiest first always' a

items.title: Evaporation causes cooling
items.keyIdea: Evaporation cools the remaining liquid because the fastest particles are the ones most likely to escape as vapour, so the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind falls and the temperature drops. That is evaporative cooling — distinct from the water-cycle story of where evaporated water g

items.title: Calculating wave speed (v = fλ)
items.keyIdea: Wave speed v equals frequency f times wavelength λ (v = f × λ). Rearrange to λ = v ÷ f or f = v ÷ λ. Convert to Hz and metres before calculating so the product is in m/s.

items.title: Interpreting parts of an expression in context
items.keyIdea: In a formula that models a situation, each term, factor and coefficient has a meaning. Read 3 + 1.5m as flag fall plus rate per mile; read P(1 + r)ⁿ with P as start and (1 + r) as the growth factor treated as one quantity.

items.title: Analysing an unseen poem
items.keyIdea: On a first-read poem under time pressure: sum the gist, name speaker and situation, pin tone with evidence, then link two language/form/sound choices to effects that support one clear overall interpretation.

items.title: 10 More or 10 Less
items.keyIdea: To find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number, change the tens digit by 1 and keep the ones digit the same: 10 more than 56 is 66, and 10 less is 46. On a hundred square, 10 more is the number straight below and 10 less is straight above, so there is no need to count on in ones.

items.title: Magnetic Poles
items.keyIdea: Every magnet has two poles, a north pole (N) and a south pole (S), where its pull is strongest. A freely hanging magnet turns until its north pole points north. When two magnets meet, like poles repel (N and N, or S and S, push apart) and unlike poles attract (N and S pull together).

items.title: Trends in properties of alkanes
items.keyIdea: As alkane chains get longer, the intermolecular forces between molecules get stronger because there is more surface contact. items.title: Advanced material properties
items.keyIdea: Group materials by tested properties: conductivity, magnetism, hardness, solubility and transparency decide what each is used for.

items.title: Place value of each digit
items.keyIdea: In a four-digit number each digit sits in a place: thousands, hundreds, tens or ones. The place sets the digit's value, so in 7,345 the 7 is worth 7000, the 3 is worth 300, the 4 is worth 40 and the 5 is worth 5. Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right, and a 0 holds an empty place (3,05

items.title: The Digestive System
items.keyIdea: Food passes through the digestive system in order: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. Teeth and saliva break food into small wet pieces; muscles in the oesophagus squeeze it down; the stomach churns it with acid into a thick soup; in the small intestine nutrients pass thro

items.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
items.keyIdea: A reversible reaction (⇌) can go both ways: reactants form products and products re-form reactants. In a closed system it reaches dynamic equilibrium: the forward and backward reactions keep going at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
