items.title: Calculating kinetic energy
items.keyIdea: Kinetic energy KE = ½ m v² with mass in kg and speed in m/s, giving joules. Square the speed, keep the half, and rearrange with v = √(2 KE / m). Doubling speed multiplies KE by four because of v².

items.title: Alternating and direct current
items.keyIdea: Direct current (d.c.) from cells and batteries keeps one direction; alternating current (a.c.) from the mains reverses each half-cycle. UK mains is about 230 V at 50 Hz. Read pd–time graphs: flat for d.c., waving through zero for a.c.

items.title: Factorising a difference of two squares
items.keyIdea: Expressions of the form a² − b² factorise as (a + b)(a − b). Both terms must be perfect squares with a minus between them. Handle coefficients such as 9x² − 25 as (3x + 5)(3x − 5). Sums like x² + 49 do not use this pattern over the reals.

items.title: Comparing and ordering numbers
items.keyIdea: Compare two two-digit numbers by place value: look at the tens digit first, then the ones if the tens match. Write the result with >, = or <, and order a set from smallest to largest the same way.

items.title: Fast & Slow Earth Changes
items.keyIdea: Earth's surface changes in two speeds: fast changes like volcanic eruptions and earthquakes happen in seconds or minutes, and slow changes like wind and water wearing rock away (erosion) take years.

items.title: Fluent adding and subtracting within 20
items.keyIdea: Fluent within 20 means you know from memory every sum of two one-digit numbers, and the related take-aways, using doubles and near-doubles as anchors — without recounting every counter each time.

items.title: Simple Chance Experiments
items.keyIdea: A chance experiment repeats a trial, like a coin flip or a dice roll, and records each outcome in a tally. The expected number is trials × chance: 20 flips × ½ = 10 heads. Real results wobble around it, the coin has no memory of a streak, and more trials give a share closer to the expected one.

items.title: Drawing particle diagrams
items.keyIdea: Draw particles as same-sized circles: neat and touching in solids, touching but jumbled in liquids, far apart and fast in gases.

items.title: Friction & Surfaces
items.keyIdea: Friction is a force between two surfaces that rub together. It always acts against the motion. Rough surfaces like carpet and sandpaper make more friction than smooth ones like ice, so a toy car given the same push stops sooner on a rough floor.

items.title: Asking scientific questions
items.keyIdea: Scientists ask how, why and where questions about the world. There are different ways to find out the answers: watch something change over time, do a test, or look it up in a book or ask an expert. A question about what you like best is not one science can answer.

items.title: Contact & Non-Contact Forces
items.keyIdea: Some forces only work when two things touch: a kick, a push on a door, friction. These are contact forces. Other forces act across a gap: a magnet pulls a paper clip before it touches it, and gravity pulls a falling apple. These are non-contact forces, and they get weaker as the gap grows.

items.title: What Plants Need to Grow
items.keyIdea: A plant needs water, light and warmth to grow and stay well. With no water it dries up and flops. In the dark it goes pale and weak. In the cold it hardly grows. Too much water is bad too, because the roots sit in water.

items.title: Rounding to 10, 100, 1000
items.keyIdea: To round a number, find the two multiples it sits between and choose the nearer one. Look at the digit just right of the place you round to: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down. So 4,367 is 4,370 to the nearest 10, 4,400 to the nearest 100 and 4,000 to the nearest 1000.

items.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines
items.keyIdea: A horizontal line lies flat, like the ground, and a vertical line goes straight up and down. Parallel lines go the same way and keep the same gap all along, so they never meet. Perpendicular lines meet or cross at a right angle, a square corner. Length and tilt do not matter: two slanted lines can b

items.title: Rainforest Layers
items.keyIdea: A rainforest has four layers. From the ground up, they are the forest floor, the understory, the canopy and the emergent layer. The floor is dark and damp, with rotting leaves. Small trees and bushes grow in the shady understory. The canopy is a thick roof of treetops, and most animals live there be

items.title: Reading Food Web Diagrams
items.keyIdea: A food web is many food chains joined together. Each arrow points from the food to the eater. Every chain starts with a producer, a plant that makes food from sunlight. items.title: Gravity & Falling Objects
items.keyIdea: Gravity is a pulling force between the Earth and every object. It pulls things towards the centre of the Earth all the time. items.title: Material properties vocabulary
items.keyIdea: Use exact words in pairs: transparent/translucent/opaque, conductor/insulator, soluble/insoluble, flexible/rigid, magnetic/non-magnetic.

items.title: Living, Dead & Never Alive
items.keyIdea: Everything belongs to one of three groups. Living things are alive now: they eat or drink, grow and have babies. items.keyIdea: Animals have babies in two main ways. Birds, reptiles, most fish, frogs and insects lay eggs, and the babies hatch out. items.title: Reading tables
items.keyIdea: A table sorts information into rows and columns. In a bus timetable each column is one bus and each row is one stop, so you go down the bus's column to the stop's row and read the time. A dash means the bus does not stop there. items.keyIdea: Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is changed, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. items.title: Linear number sequences
items.keyIdea: A linear sequence uses the same step from each term to the next. That step is the term-to-term rule. It can add, take away, or use a decimal, such as +4, −3 or +0.5. The 10th term is the first term plus 9 of those steps, not 10. If the step changes, as in 2, 4, 8, 16, the sequence is not linear.

items.title: Animal Migration
items.keyIdea: Migration is a long trip an animal makes, and then it comes back. Animals travel to find food, to have babies, or to follow the seasons. items.title: Levers, Pulleys & Gears
items.keyIdea: Levers, pulleys and gears can let a smaller force have a greater effect. On a lever, push farther from the pivot than the load sits. items.keyIdea: Each statistics word names one job. Frequency counts how often a value comes up. The mode is the most common value. The median is the middle value once the data is in order. items.title: Savanna & Grassland Animals
items.keyIdea: A grassland is a wide open habitat of grass with few trees. The African savanna has lions, zebras, wildebeest, elephants, giraffes and cheetahs. items.title: Reading and drawing circuit diagrams
items.keyIdea: A circuit diagram uses standard symbols instead of pictures. A cell is a long thin line and a short thick line. A battery is two or more cells joined. A lamp is a circle with a cross. items.title: Place value: × 10 and ÷ 10
items.keyIdea: Each place is worth ten times the place to its right, so × 10 moves every digit one place left and ÷ 10 moves it one place right.

items.title: Times tables for 2, 5 and 10
items.keyIdea: A times table fact like 5 × 3 = 15 tells you how many are in equal groups. The 10s facts all end in 0. The 5s facts are half of the 10s facts. The 2s facts are doubles. Each times fact gives a division fact too: 5 × 3 = 15, so 15 ÷ 5 = 3 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Those facts make a fact family.

items.title: Times tables for 3, 4 and 8
items.keyIdea: The 4s are double the 2s, and the 8s are double the 4s: 2 × 7 = 14, 4 × 7 = 28, 8 × 7 = 56. The 3s are 2 lots and 1 more lot: 3 × 8 = 16 + 8 = 24. Every times fact gives a division fact: 8 × 4 = 32, so 32 ÷ 4 = 8. Every 8s number is a 4s number, but only every other 4s number is an 8s number.

items.title: Desert Animals
items.keyIdea: A desert is a habitat with very little rain or snow, under about 250 mm a year. Deserts can be hot or cold, but they are always dry. items.title: Fractions as division
items.keyIdea: a/b means a ÷ b: sharing a wholes equally between b people gives each person a/b.

items.title: Coordinates on a grid
items.keyIdea: (x, y) means go x across along the x-axis, then y up, starting from the origin (0, 0).

items.title: Percentage increase and decrease
items.keyIdea: Use a multiplier: increase by r% means × (1 + r/100), decrease means × (1 − r/100); divide by it to find the original.

items.title: Charges and masses of subatomic particles
items.keyIdea: Protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1) sit in the tiny nucleus; electrons (−1, mass almost 0) are outside it.

items.title: Acids, alkalis and pH
items.keyIdea: pH runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline; indicators show it with colour.

items.title: Reactions that release or absorb heat
items.keyIdea: Exothermic reactions give energy out (temperature rises); endothermic reactions take energy in (temperature falls).

items.title: Reading distance–time graphs
items.keyIdea: On a distance–time graph, flat means stopped, steeper means faster, and the gradient is the speed.

items.title: Measuring temperature with negative numbers
items.keyIdea: Below zero is negative; to find a change across zero, count to zero first and then on.

items.title: Velocity–time graphs
items.keyIdea: On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration and the area underneath is the displacement.

items.title: Net change as accumulated rate
items.keyIdea: The signed area under any rate graph is the net change in the quantity; area below the axis counts as a decrease.

items.title: Physical meaning of gradient and area
items.keyIdea: The gradient of a graph is a rate (speed, acceleration, power); the area under a graph is an accumulated amount (distance, energy).

items.title: Polynomial vocabulary
items.keyIdea: A polynomial is a sum of terms; its degree is the highest power, and standard form lists terms from highest power to lowest.

items.title: Laws of exponents
items.keyIdea: When you multiply powers of the same base you add the powers, when you divide you subtract them, and a power of a power multiplies them.

items.title: Zero and negative exponents
items.keyIdea: Each step down in the power divides by the base, so a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.

items.title: Fractional exponents and radicals
items.keyIdea: a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) is that root raised to the power m.

items.title: Solving x² = p and x³ = p
items.keyIdea: x² = p has two solutions, ±√p, when p is positive; x³ = p has exactly one, ∛p.

items.title: What makes a function
items.keyIdea: A function gives exactly one output for each input.

items.title: Multiplying polynomials
items.keyIdea: To multiply polynomials, multiply every term in one by every term in the other, then collect like terms.

items.title: Adding and subtracting polynomials
items.keyIdea: Add or subtract polynomials by combining like terms; when subtracting, change the sign of every term in the second polynomial.

items.title: Acceleration
items.keyIdea: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes: a = change in velocity ÷ time, measured in m/s².

items.title: Displacement and velocity in a line
items.keyIdea: Displacement is how far you end up from the start in a chosen direction; average velocity is displacement ÷ time.

items.title: Key features of graphs
items.keyIdea: Read a graph's story from its features: intercepts, where it rises or falls, its highest and lowest points, symmetry and end behaviour.

items.title: Sketching and describing qualitative graphs
items.keyIdea: A graph without numbers can still tell a story: rising, falling, flat, steeper or levelling off.

items.title: Scalars and vectors
items.keyIdea: A scalar has only a size; a vector has a size and a direction.

items.title: What is a half?
items.keyIdea: A half is one of two equal parts.

items.title: Finding halves and quarters
items.keyIdea: A quarter is one of four equal parts; two quarters make a half.

items.title: Objects and materials
items.keyIdea: An object is a thing; a material is what the thing is made of.

items.title: Naming everyday materials
items.keyIdea: Everyday things are made of materials such as wood, plastic, glass, metal, rock and fabric.

items.title: Describing material properties
items.keyIdea: We describe materials with pairs of words: hard or soft, stiff or bendy, shiny or dull, waterproof or not.

items.title: Choosing the right material
items.keyIdea: We choose a material because its properties suit the job.

items.title: Grouping materials
items.keyIdea: We can group materials by a property, such as hard or soft, or shiny or dull.

items.title: Solid, liquid and gas words
items.keyIdea: A solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill any space.

items.title: Solids, liquids and gases
items.keyIdea: We group materials as solids, liquids or gases by how they behave: keep shape, flow, or spread out.

items.title: Heating and cooling changes
items.keyIdea: Heating can melt a solid and boil a liquid; cooling can freeze a liquid; we measure the temperature in °C.

items.title: Dissolving and solutions
items.keyIdea: Some solids dissolve in water to make a solution; we get the solid back by evaporating the water.
